newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-PRESS DIGEST-Australian General News - Feb 12.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-PRESS DIGEST-Australian General News - Feb 12.

text.p: (Compiled for Reuters by Media Monitors)
THE AUSTRALIAN FINANCIAL REVIEW

The housing industry has started to recover from its recent slump, but, according to Australian Bureau of Statistics figures released yesterday, banks are losing their stranglehold on the mortgage market, with the number of loans for housing rising 5.3 per cent in December, seasonally adjusted, to stand 7.4 per cent higher than a year ago. Page 1.

Alarmed at the 25 per cent increase in calls to its free 013 service, Telstra has proposed a 50 cent directory assistance charge, which will target some business users and "Generation X'ers". The national telecommunications carrier believes the model will help stem a A$210 million black hole in its accounts before privatisation. Page 3.

Correspondence supplied to senators has revealed Prime Minister John Howard approved a pay rise worth A$23,000 for Mrs Smith, a staffer to Independent Senator Mal Colston, just 12 days before Senator Colston provided one of two crucial votes to pass the Calition's Telstra sale through the Senate. Page 3.

For the second time in two weeks, Prime Minister John Howard went into damage control yesterday when he admitted to Parliament he had inadvertently misled the Australian public over the Government's hastily devised work-for-the-dole scheme. Howard conceded that he had previously ruled out such a scheme during the election campaign, despite assurances to Parliament on Monday that he had not. Page 5.
THE AUSTRALIAN

The Howard Government is under increasing pressure from Government MPs to give smaller States a larger role in its planned People's Convention on the republic after proposing far greater representation for the larger States, with New South Wales set to have three times the number of elected delegates than Tasmania. Page 1.

Following claims by Prime Minister John Howard on Monday that he had been careful not to rule out schemes like the work-for-the-dole plan during the 1996 Federal election, Prime Minister John Howard admitted yesterday, in a response to a newspaper questionaire, that the Liberal Party had ruled out the schemes under his name during the election. Page 1.

Under a A$50 million proposal being put forward by Telstra, in a move which defies the Federal Government's election promise that directory assistance calls will remain free, consumers face a 50 cent charge every time they dial the 013 directory assistance service. The plan was unveiled late yesterday after details were leaked to Opposition Communications Spokesman Chris Schacht. Page 1.

In a decision which Norman Rosenbaum says is an important step forward in the treatment of race-related crimes in the United States, two men have been convicted of violating the human rights of his brother, 29-year-old Melbourne University student Yankel Rosenbaum, who was killed during the race riots that roared through New York's Crown Heights five-and-a-half years ago. Page 1.
THE SYDNEY MORNING HERALD

All NSW teachers have been ordered to undergo training in how to teach children to read and write following NSW Education Minister John Aquilina admitting the system had failed a large number of students. Up to 60,000 teachers will undergo the specialist training as a part of an A$18.4 million literacy strategy. Page 1.

It has been revealed that Prime Minister Howard personally approved additional "perks" for independent Senator Mal Colston and his staff worth up to $75,000 in the lead-up to the Senate vote on the part-privatisation of Telstra. In a move which was outside the normal guidelines for pay increases, Howard approved a substantial pay rise for a junior Colston staff member. Page 1.

The NSW Cabinet has decided to pull out of the national legal aid system and fund only cases brought under NSW laws. The move has placed pressure on the Federal Government, which is cutting the national legal aid budget by A$120 million, to pick up the tab for defendants charged under Commonwealth laws. Page 1.

A Senate-styled voting system, with electors being allowed to vote for tickets "above-the-line" has been proposed to select 76 of the 152 delegates for this year's People's Convention on the Republic. However the complicated voting plan has come under fire from the smaller states, claiming the convention risks being dominated by the larger Victoria and NSW. Page 3.
THE AGE

Following the release of the recommendations of the first review of the television industry's codes of practice since the industry began self-regulation in 1993, there will be tougher classifications for violent programs, restricted news coverage of brutal events and tragedies, and a ban on children's programs advertising products. Page A1.

Police last night charged a 28-year-old Carlton man with failing to give way, stop, render assistance, exchange names and addresses and with not reporting an accident over the hit-and-run death of Brian Stacey, the 49-year-old musical conductor and director of Sunset Boulevard. Page A1.

The Victorian Casino and Gaming Authority has been ordered by the Administrative Appeals Tribunal to make public a list of documents, containing financial information about the rival bids, that passed between the Authority and the State Government during the Casino tendering process. Page A1.

Victoria's public health crisis worsened yesterday, with confirmation that a 40-year-old man was being treated for anthrax in Kyabram in the State's west. Reports of the first human infection of the disease came as anthrax was discovered in several more dairy herds in the Tatura region. Page A2.
-- Reuters Sydney Newsroom 61-2 9373-1800
